content: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection that is particularly common in children. There is no universally accepted standard treatment for this condition, and treatment guidelines vary significantly. Available treatment options include a variety of oral and topical antibiotics, as well as disinfectants. This review is an updated version of the original analysis published in 2003. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various treatments for impetigo, including non-pharmacological approaches and the option of allowing the condition to resolve naturally. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated treatments for different forms of impetigo, including non-bullous, bullous, primary, and secondary types. The search for relevant studies was updated to July 2010, covering multiple databases such as the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS. Ongoing trials were identified through online trial registries, and reference lists of newly identified studies were manually reviewed. Data collection and quality assessments were conducted independently by two authors in separate stages. A total of 68 trials involving 5,578 participants were included in this updated review, examining 50 different treatments, including placebo. Most trials focused on primary impetigo or did not specify the type of impetigo. However, many studies lacked sufficient information to assess the risk of bias. Only 15 studies reported blinding of participants and outcome assessors. Topical antibiotic treatments demonstrated higher cure rates compared to placebo, as evidenced by pooled data from six studies involving 575 participants (risk ratio [RR] 2.24, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.61 to 3.13). Among the most commonly studied topical antibiotics, mupirocin and fusidic acid, there was no clear evidence of one being more effective than the other, based on four studies with 440 participants (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.11). Topical mupirocin was found to be slightly more effective than oral erythromycin in 10 studies with 581 participants (pooled RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.13). However, there were no significant differences in cure rates when comparing topical antibiotics to other oral antibiotics. Differences were observed among oral antibiotics, with penicillin being less effective than erythromycin (pooled RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.56, based on two studies with 79 participants) and cloxacillin (pooled RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.21 to 2.08, based on two studies with 166 participants). There was insufficient evidence to support the use of disinfectant solutions for treating impetigo. When data from two studies with 292 participants were pooled, topical antibiotics were shown to be significantly more effective than disinfectant treatments (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.32). Reported side effects were generally low in number and mild in severity. However, oral antibiotic treatments were associated with a higher incidence of side effects compared to topical treatments, with gastrointestinal symptoms being the most commonly reported adverse effects. Globally, there is increasing bacterial resistance to commonly used antibiotics for impetigo. However, no resistance has been reported for the newly developed topical antibiotic, retapamulin. In conclusion, there is strong evidence that topical mupirocin and fusidic acid are equally effective and, in some cases, more effective than oral antibiotics for treating impetigo. However, due to a lack of studies involving individuals with extensive impetigo, it remains unclear whether oral antibiotics are superior in such cases. Fusidic acid and mupirocin have comparable efficacy, while penicillin is less effective than most other antibiotics. There is limited evidence to support the use of disinfectant solutions for managing impetigo.
